title: Marcus Aurelius’s Meditations were private notes he probably never meant anyone to read

cover.alt: A bronze equestrian statue of the emperor Marcus Aurelius with his arm outstretched, on a plinth on the Capitoline Hill in Rome; the outdoor statue is a replica of the ancient original.

body: The Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius wrote the twelve books now called the Meditations in Greek, mostly between 170 and 180 AD, much of it while campaigning on the Danube frontier: one book notes it was written in the country of the Quadi, another at Carnuntum. The work has no real title; the Greek manuscripts call it Ta eis heauton, ‘things to himself’. It is unlikely he ever intended it to be published. It survived by luck, through a copy mentioned before 907 and two main manuscripts, one of which is now lost, and was first printed in Zürich in 1558 or 1559.

slides.alt: The Heidentor, a ruined Roman monumental arch of rough stone standing alone in a field at Carnuntum, Austria.
slides.caption: The Heidentor at Carnuntum, the Roman base on the Danube where Marcus notes he wrote the second book of the Meditations.

slides.prompt: What did Marcus call the book?
slides.detail: The Greek manuscripts head it Ta eis heauton, ‘things to himself’. ‘Meditations’ is a label given much later.

steps.label: A copy sent by Arethas before 907
Two main manuscripts; one now lost

slides.heading: A thin thread
slides.text: The text rests almost entirely on two sources: a manuscript that Xylander printed from in 1558–59 and that has since been lost, and a corrupt 14th-century copy in the Vatican Library that is missing about 42 lines. Two other manuscripts hold only extracts.

slides.question: In what language did the Roman emperor write his private notes?
slides.explanation: He wrote in Koine Greek rather than Latin. The twelve books were mostly written between 170 and 180 AD.
